title: Gordon Allport: Motivation and Personality
overview: Gordon Allport made personality an academically respectable topic with his 1937 book and built a trait theory centred on the unique individual. Rejecting Freud, he held that healthy adults are conscious, rational and guided by present and future goals, not childhood conflicts. He defined personality as the dynamic organization of psychophysical systems that determine characteristic behaviour and thought, distinguished common traits from personal dispositions (cardinal, central and secondary), and proposed functional autonomy: adult motives become independent of their origins, at perseverative and propriate levels. The self, or proprium, develops through seven stages from infancy to adolescence, depending on the infant-mother bond, and the mature adult meets six criteria of health. Allport assessed personality with personal documents (the Jenny letters) and the Study of Values, and studied expressive behaviour, which later research on facial expressions, culture and computer recognition has extended. Critics note the theory is hard to test and over-stresses uniqueness and discontinuity, but it influenced humanistic psychology.
objectives: Explain how Allport made personality an academically respectable field and how his theory differs from Freud's.
Relate Allport's childhood, his rivalry with Floyd and his meeting with Freud to his theory.
Define personality in Allport's terms and explain the roles of heredity, environment and discontinuity.
Describe the characteristics of traits and distinguish common traits from personal dispositions (cardinal, central, secondary).
Explain functional autonomy, its perseverative and propriate levels, and the three principles of propriate functioning.
Describe the proprium and its seven stages of development, and the role of the infant-mother bond.
List and explain Allport's six criteria of the healthy adult personality and his view of human nature.
Describe the personal-document technique and the Study of Values.
Summarise research on expressive behaviour, facial expressions, cultural differences and computer recognition.
Evaluate Allport's theory, including criticisms and its influence.

sections.heading: Allport Brings Personality into the Classroom and the Psychology Lab
sections.detailed:
Over a career of more than forty years, Gordon Allport did something no earlier theorist in the book had managed: he made personality a respectable academic subject. Freud's psychoanalysis and the neo-psychoanalytic theories that grew out of it (Jung, Adler, Horney and others) had developed largely in clinics and consulting rooms. Mainstream scientific psychology, which was experimental and university-based, did not treat them as part of its own territory.

The turning point came in 1937, when Allport published Personality: A Psychological Interpretation. Until then the psychology establishment had not accepted the formal, systematic study of personality as a legitimate field. The book was an instant success and became a classic of personality psychology. It defined personality as something that could be studied in university departments and taught in classrooms.

The chapter therefore credits Allport with two achievements. First, he moved personality from the margins into the mainstream of academic psychology. Second, he built his own theory of personality development in which traits occupy a central place. This is why Allport is placed in the book's "genetics approach" (trait approach) section: he gave traits, and the genetic raw material behind them, a major role in explaining individual personality.

For exam purposes, remember the date (1937), the book title, and the two-fold contribution. Later in the chapter (Reflections) the authors return to this point, describing Allport's most lasting legacy as making personality study academically respectable and stressing genetic factors within a trait approach. So this opening section and the final evaluation frame the whole chapter.
sections.simple: Allport made personality an accepted topic in university psychology. Before his 1937 book, psychoanalytic theories were seen as outside scientific psychology. He also created a theory of personality built around traits.
keyPoints: Psychoanalytic theories were not considered part of mainstream scientific psychology.
Allport's 1937 book Personality: A Psychological Interpretation won formal recognition for personality study.
The book became an immediate success and a classic.
Two contributions: bringing personality into the mainstream and a trait-based theory of development.

sections.heading: Allport Challenges Freud
sections.detailed:
Allport rejected Freud's psychoanalysis on three main points, and these contrasts run through the whole chapter.

1. The role of the unconscious. Freud held that unconscious forces dominate personality. Allport denied that this is true of normal, mature adults. In his view, emotionally healthy people operate rationally and consciously; they are aware of, and can control, many of the forces that motivate them. The unconscious matters, he said, only for neurotic or disturbed people.

2. Historical determinism. Historical determinism is the idea that the past determines the present. Freud believed adults are shaped by childhood conflicts and experiences. Allport argued that we are not prisoners of our past; we are guided more by the present and by how we see the future. He famously complained that people are busy living toward the future while psychology is busy tracing them back into the past (Allport, 1955).

3. The use of abnormal subjects. Freud built his theory largely on data from neurotic patients and saw normal and abnormal behaviour as lying on one continuum. Allport saw a sharp break between the two. For him the abnormal personality functions at an infantile level. The only proper way to study personality was to gather data from emotionally healthy adults. Neurotics, children and animals should not be compared with normal adults, because Allport saw no functional similarity in personality between child and adult, abnormal and normal, or animal and human.

These three positions explain Allport's later ideas: functional autonomy (adult motives are independent of childhood), the two discontinuous personalities of childhood and adulthood, the emphasis on conscious intentions and future goals, and his reluctance to use case histories and projective tests. They also give rise to the main criticism of his theory: that research on children, animals and disturbed people has in fact taught us much about normal adults.
sections.simple: Allport disagreed with Freud on three things. Healthy adults are mostly conscious and rational, not ruled by the unconscious; we are guided by the present and future rather than trapped by childhood; and personality should be studied in healthy adults, not neurotics, children or animals.
keyPoints: Unconscious forces matter only in neurotic or disturbed people, not in healthy adults.
Rejected historical determinism: present and future guide us more than the past.
Saw a clear break, not a continuum, between normal and abnormal; the abnormal personality is infantile.
Only emotionally healthy adults should be studied; no functional similarity between child/adult, abnormal/normal, animal/human.

sections.heading: Allport Makes Each Person Unique
sections.detailed:
A second defining feature of Allport's theory is its insistence that every personality is unique, and that this uniqueness is defined by the particular traits each person has.

Traditional science aims to discover general constructs and universal laws that apply to everyone. Allport resisted this emphasis when it came to personality. He argued that personality is not general or universal; it is particular and specific to each individual. Two people might both be described as "anxious" or "friendly", but the way those characteristics are organised and expressed in each person is distinctive.

This principle shapes much of the rest of the chapter. It explains why Allport later separated individual traits (personal dispositions) from common traits, and why he considered personal dispositions the more accurate description of a person. It explains his stress on genetic endowment as the main source of uniqueness, since no two people (except identical twins) share the same genes and no two people share exactly the same environment. It also explains his research preference: he favoured the idiographic approach, the intensive study of the single case (for example, the analysis of Jenny's letters), over the nomothetic approach of averaging across large groups, although he used nomothetic tests such as the Study of Values when appropriate.

The emphasis on uniqueness is also one of the main targets of criticism. Critics argue that if every person is studied only as a unique case, it becomes impossible to generalise from one person to another, which is the usual aim of science. Allport's uniqueness emphasis ran against the dominant nomothetic trend of the psychology of his time, and this partly explains why his theory as a whole has stimulated relatively little research.
sections.simple: Allport believed every personality is one-of-a-kind, defined by that person's own pattern of traits. He resisted the scientific habit of looking for universal laws that apply to everyone.
keyPoints: Uniqueness of personality is defined by each person's traits.
Opposed the scientific emphasis on general constructs and universal laws for personality.
Personality is particular and specific to the individual.
Leads to his preference for the idiographic study of individual cases.
Later criticised because it makes generalising from one person to another impossible.

sections.heading: The Life of Allport (1897-1967): Restrictions, Isolation and Inferiority
sections.detailed:
Restrictions, morality and no bright colours. Gordon Allport was born in Montezuma, Indiana, the youngest of four sons. His mother was a teacher; his father, a salesman, decided to become a doctor. While the father attended medical school in Baltimore the family was so poor that he smuggled drugs from Canada and sold them; when the police arrived he escaped over the back fence and moved the family to Indiana, where he set up a private practice. Allport believed his own birth was his father's first case. Home life was dominated by his mother's devout religion: no smoking, drinking, dancing or card playing, and no bright colours, distinctive clothes or jewellery. She was strict, with firm ideas of right and wrong (Nicholson, 2003).

Isolation and rejection. Allport was too young to play with his older brothers and was also cut off from other children. He said he built his own small circle of activities because he never fitted in with the general crowd of boys. He suffered on the playground, did not get along with his brothers, felt they disliked him and saw them as more masculine than himself. He described himself as good with words but poor at sports and games, and as someone who worked hard to be the centre of attention among his few friends. Interestingly, his theory holds that healthy adults are unaffected by childhood events, and he revealed very little about his own childhood; yet what he did reveal parallels the theory he developed.

Inferiority. Isolation and rejection produced inferiority feelings, which he tried to compensate for by striving to excel (an idea reminiscent of Adler). He described an identity quest arising from feeling inferior to his brothers and other children. He came to identify with and envy his oldest brother, Floyd, followed him to Harvard and, like Floyd, earned a Ph.D. in psychology. Floyd became a noted social psychologist, and even as Gordon grew famous he felt he was in his brother's shadow; at 31 he wrote that he should not be confused with his "more eminent brother".

The link to his theory. The book suggests that imitating Floyd may have threatened Gordon's sense of identity. To assert his individuality, he may have been motivated to deny that his adult motives and interests had anything to do with his childhood feelings, an idea he later formalised as functional autonomy. This is a key answer to Review Question 1.
sections.simple: Allport grew up the youngest of four sons in a strict, religious household. Isolated and rejected by his brothers, he felt inferior and tried to compensate by excelling, especially by copying his eldest brother Floyd. Wanting to be his own person may have led him to argue that adult motives are independent of childhood, the idea of functional autonomy.
keyPoints: Born in Montezuma, Indiana, youngest of four sons; strict, devout mother; no bright colours or pleasures allowed.
Isolated from brothers and other children; good with words, poor at sports.
Inferiority feelings led to striving to excel and an identity quest.
Identified with and envied eldest brother Floyd, following him to Harvard and a psychology Ph.D.
Desire to assert individuality may underlie the concept of functional autonomy.

sections.heading: The Life of Allport: College Years, Meeting Freud and Becoming a Success
sections.detailed:
College years. Although Allport finished second in a high school class of 100, he was unsure what to do next. At the end of summer 1915 he applied to Harvard and was accepted, saying his world was remade overnight. Shocked by poor grades on his first exams, he doubled his efforts and ended the year with straight A's. His parents' interest in social ethics and service was strengthened at Harvard: he volunteered at a boys' club, with factory workers and with foreign students, and worked as a probation officer. He enjoyed helping people because it gave him a feeling of competence that offset his general sense of inferiority, and he saw this service as part of his search for identity. He took some psychology courses without planning a career in it, and graduated in 1919, on the same day Floyd received his Ph.D. He then taught for a year at Robert College in Istanbul, Turkey, before accepting a Harvard fellowship for graduate study in psychology; his biographer notes that becoming more like his successful brother appealed to him (Nicholson, 2003).

Allport meets Freud. Returning to the US, he stopped in Vienna and wrote to Freud, who invited him to visit. Freud waited silently for the young man to explain himself. Uncomfortable, Allport described a small boy he had just seen on the streetcar who was afraid of dirt and asked his mother not to let a dirty man sit beside him. Freud looked at the neat, carefully groomed visitor and asked whether that little boy was Allport himself, implying the story revealed Allport's own unconscious fears. Freud saw him as neat, orderly and punctual, traits he associated with the compulsive personality (Pervin, 1984); another psychologist said Freud had hit the nail on the head (Anderson, 1990). Allport denied it all his life but called the encounter traumatic (Allport, 1967). He concluded that psychoanalysis probes the unconscious too deeply and that psychology should focus on conscious, visible motives, the path his theory took. Later, Kaufman and Bristol (2001) used this anecdote to show that personal, social stories make lectures more enjoyable and help students learn and remember.

Becoming a success. Allport finished his Harvard Ph.D. in 1922 after two years. His dissertation, An Experimental Study of the Traits of Personality, was the first research on personality traits ever conducted in the United States. After two years on a travelling fellowship in Germany and England he returned to Harvard as an instructor and taught what was apparently the first formal American college course on personality. He spent nearly four decades at Harvard. His honours included the American Psychological Foundation's Gold Medal, the APA's Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award, and the presidencies of the APA and the Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues.
sections.simple: At Harvard Allport worked hard, did social service that made him feel competent, and eventually chose psychology. An awkward meeting with Freud, who suggested Allport himself was the dirt-fearing boy in his story, convinced him to focus on conscious motives. He wrote the first US study of personality traits, taught the first US personality course and became a leading figure in psychology.
keyPoints: Entered Harvard in 1915; straight A's after poor first exams; social service offset inferiority and aided identity search.
Graduated 1919 (same day as Floyd's Ph.D.); taught at Robert College, Istanbul.
Freud's question 'Was that little boy you?' left a traumatic impression; Allport turned to conscious motivation.
Ph.D. 1922: first US research on personality traits; first formal US college course on personality.
Nearly 40 years at Harvard; APF Gold Medal, APA Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award, APA president.

sections.heading: The Nature of Personality
sections.detailed:
Allport's definition. In Pattern and Growth in Personality (1961), Allport examined about 50 existing definitions before proposing his own: personality is the dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine characteristic behaviour and thought. Each part of the definition carries meaning:
- Dynamic organization: personality is constantly changing and growing, but the growth is organised, not random.
- Psychophysical: personality consists of mind and body working together as one unit; it is neither purely mental nor purely biological.
- Determine: every aspect of personality activates or directs specific behaviours and thoughts.
- Characteristic behaviour and thought: everything we think and do is typical of us, which is why each person is unique.

The roles of heredity and environment. To support his emphasis on uniqueness, Allport said personality reflects both heredity and environment. Heredity supplies the raw materials, such as physique, intelligence and temperament, which environmental conditions then shape, expand or limit. He therefore used both personal and situational variables, acknowledging both genetics and learning. However, genetic background accounts for the major share of our uniqueness. The number of possible gene combinations is effectively infinite, and except for identical twins the chance of anyone duplicating another's genetic endowment is negligible. Genes also interact with the social environment, and no two people, not even siblings raised in the same house, have exactly the same environment. The inevitable result is a unique personality, so Allport argued that psychology must study the individual case rather than average findings across groups.

Two distinct personalities for two stages of life. Allport considered personality discrete or discontinuous. Each person differs from everyone else, and each adult is also cut off from his or her own past. There is no continuum between childhood and adult personality. Infants are driven by primitive biological urges and reflexes, while adult functioning is mainly psychological. In effect there are two personalities, one for childhood and one for adulthood, and the adult personality is not constrained by childhood experience.

Summary of his position. This view stresses the conscious over the unconscious, the present and future over the past, uniqueness over generalities about large groups, and the normal rather than the abnormal personality. These four emphases summarise how Allport stands apart from Freud.
sections.simple: Allport defined personality as the dynamic organization of mind-body (psychophysical) systems inside a person that produce his or her typical behaviour and thought. Heredity gives the raw material and environment shapes it, with genes the main source of uniqueness. He also held that child and adult personalities are separate: the adult is not bound by childhood.
keyPoints: Definition: dynamic organization within the individual of psychophysical systems that determine characteristic behaviour and thought.
Dynamic = organised growth; psychophysical = mind and body as a unit; characteristic = typical of each person.
Heredity supplies physique, intelligence and temperament; environment shapes them; genes give most of our uniqueness.
Psychology must study the individual case, not group averages.
Personality is discontinuous: one personality for childhood (biological) and one for adulthood (psychological).

sections.heading: Personality Traits
sections.detailed:
Allport defined traits as predispositions to respond in the same or a similar way to different kinds of stimuli. Put simply, traits are consistent and enduring ways of reacting to the environment. The margin definition describes them as distinguishing characteristics that guide behaviour, measured on a continuum and subject to social, environmental and cultural influences.

Allport (1937) summarised the characteristics of traits as follows:
1. Traits are real and exist within each person. They are not theoretical constructs or labels invented to explain behaviour.
2. Traits determine or cause behaviour. They do not merely appear in response to stimuli; they motivate us to seek appropriate stimuli and interact with the environment to produce behaviour.
3. Traits can be demonstrated empirically. By observing a person's behaviour over time we can infer a trait from the consistency of responses to the same or similar stimuli.
4. Traits are interrelated and may overlap even though they are different characteristics. Aggressiveness and hostility, for example, are distinct but related and often occur together.
5. Traits vary with the situation. A person may be neat in one situation and disorderly in another.

(Review Question 4 asks for four characteristics; any four of these five can be given, but it is safer to know all five.)

Individual versus common traits. Allport initially proposed two types of trait. Individual traits are unique to one person and define his or her character. Common traits are shared by a number of people, for example the members of a culture. It follows that people in different cultures will have different common traits, and that common traits will change over time as social standards and values change. This shows that common traits are subject to social, environmental and cultural influences.

The distinction between individual and common traits reflects Allport's balance between uniqueness and comparison: common traits allow us to compare people within a culture, while individual traits capture what is truly distinctive about a person. As the next section explains, Allport later renamed these to avoid confusion.
sections.simple: Traits are lasting tendencies to react in similar ways across different situations. Allport said traits are real, cause behaviour, can be observed, overlap with each other and vary with the situation. He first divided them into individual traits (unique to one person) and common traits (shared within a culture).
keyPoints: Traits: consistent, enduring predispositions to respond similarly to different stimuli.
Five characteristics: real, cause behaviour, empirically demonstrable, interrelated, vary with situation.
Individual traits are unique to a person and define character.
Common traits are shared, e.g., by members of a culture, and differ across cultures.
Common traits change as social standards and values change.

sections.heading: Personal Dispositions
sections.detailed:
Allport later realised that calling both individual and common characteristics "traits" could cause confusion, so he revised his terms. Common traits were now simply called traits, and individual traits became personal dispositions. Personal dispositions are traits peculiar to an individual, as opposed to traits shared by many people.

Not all personal dispositions are equally intense or significant. Allport distinguished three levels:

Cardinal traits. A cardinal trait is so pervasive and influential that it affects almost every aspect of a person's life. Allport called it a ruling passion, a powerful force dominating behaviour. His examples were sadism and chauvinism. Two qualifications matter: not everyone has a ruling passion, and people who do may not display it in every situation. Cardinal traits are the most powerful type and therefore exert the strongest influence on personality (relevant to Review Question 5).

Central traits. Everyone has a few central traits, about 5 to 10 themes that best describe a person's behaviour. Allport's examples were aggressiveness, self-pity and cynicism. These are the qualities we would mention when describing a friend's personality or writing a letter of recommendation. They are less pervasive than cardinal traits but more consistent and noticeable than secondary traits.

Secondary traits. These are the least influential personal dispositions. They appear much less consistently than cardinal and central traits and may be so weak or inconspicuous that only a close friend would notice them. Examples include a minor preference for a certain type of music or a particular food.

The three levels thus form a hierarchy of pervasiveness and consistency: cardinal (dominates almost everything, rare), central (a handful of key themes, universal), secondary (weak, inconsistent, peripheral). The chapter summary repeats this: cardinal traits are powerful and pervasive, central traits less pervasive, and secondary traits displayed less conspicuously and consistently than the others.
sections.simple: Allport renamed common traits simply 'traits' and individual traits 'personal dispositions'. Personal dispositions come in three strengths: a cardinal trait is a ruling passion that dominates life (not everyone has one), central traits are the 5 to 10 themes that describe a person, and secondary traits are minor preferences only close friends notice.
keyPoints: Common traits relabelled 'traits'; individual traits relabelled 'personal dispositions'.
Cardinal trait: a pervasive 'ruling passion' (e.g., sadism, chauvinism); not everyone has one.
Central traits: 5 to 10 themes everyone has (e.g., aggressiveness, self-pity, cynicism).
Secondary traits: least influential, inconsistent, e.g., minor music or food preferences.
Cardinal traits exert the most powerful influence on personality.

sections.heading: Motivation: What We Strive for
sections.detailed:
Allport believed that the central problem for any personality theory is how it handles motivation. His treatment of motivation follows directly from his emphasis on the present.

The present matters, not the past. It is a person's current state that is important, not events from toilet training, school or some other childhood crisis. What happened in the past is simply past: it is no longer active and cannot explain adult behaviour unless it still exists as a present motivating force. This contrasts directly with Freud's historical determinism.

The role of cognitive processes. Our cognitive processes, meaning our conscious plans and intentions, are a vital part of personality. Allport criticised theories like Freud's that concentrated on unconscious, irrational forces and neglected conscious, rational ones. Deliberate intentions are essential to personality. What we want and what we strive for are the keys to understanding our behaviour. This is the answer to Review Question 8 on the role of cognitive processes.

Explaining the present by the future. Because intentions and goals point forward, Allport tried to explain the present in terms of the future rather than the past. A person's behaviour today is best understood by asking what he or she is trying to achieve, not by digging into early experiences.

The relationship between personality and motivation (Review Question 6). For Allport, motivation is at the heart of personality: personality is expressed through current, conscious strivings and intentions, and the way a theory handles motivation determines its adequacy. This view leads to his best-known concept, functional autonomy, which explains how adult motives become independent of the childhood conditions in which they began. It also links to his view of human nature, in which the goal of life is to keep striving and to seek increased, not reduced, tension.
sections.simple: For Allport, how a theory explains motivation is its central problem. What drives adults is their present situation and conscious plans and goals, not childhood events. He explained present behaviour by what people are aiming for in the future.
keyPoints: Motivation is the central problem for any personality theory.
The current state matters; the past is inactive unless it is a present motivating force.
Cognitive processes (conscious plans and intentions) are vital parts of personality.
What we want and strive for is the key to understanding behaviour.
Explains the present in terms of the future, not the past.

sections.heading: Functional Autonomy: Perseverative and Propriate
sections.detailed:
The concept. Functional autonomy proposes that the motives of mature, emotionally healthy adults are not functionally connected to the earlier experiences in which they first appeared. Forces that motivated us early in life become autonomous, independent of their original circumstances. The margin definition calls it the idea that motives in the normal mature adult are independent of the childhood experiences in which they originally arose.

Allport's analogies. A tree can obviously be traced to its seed, but a fully grown tree no longer needs the seed for nourishment; it is self-determining and no longer functionally related to it. Similarly, as adults we become independent of our parents: still related to them, but no longer functionally dependent on them, and they should no longer control our lives.

The career example. New graduates may work hard for financial success and security. Eventually they may earn enough to retire, yet some keep working just as hard. The 55-year-old is not pursuing the 25-year-old's goal, which has been reached. Hard work, once a means to an end (money), has become an end in itself; the motive has become independent of its source. Therefore adult motives cannot be understood by exploring childhood, as Freud believed; we must investigate why people behave as they do today.

Two levels. Allport proposed two levels of functional autonomy.

Perseverative functional autonomy is the more elementary level. It covers addictions and repetitive physical actions such as habitual ways of performing a routine task. These behaviours persevere on their own without external reward. They once served a purpose but no longer do, and they are too basic to be an integral part of personality. Evidence: a rat trained to run a maze for food may keep running it even when well fed, clearly for some other reason; humans prefer familiar routines that they continue without external reinforcement.

Propriate functional autonomy is more important and is essential for understanding adult motivation. "Propriate" comes from proprium, Allport's term for the ego or self. It relates to our values, self-image and lifestyle. Propriate motives are unique to each person. The ego decides which motives are kept and which discarded; we retain those that enhance self-esteem or self-image. Hence there is a direct relationship between interests and abilities: we enjoy doing what we do well. A child may be forced by parents to take piano lessons; as skill grows, commitment grows. The original motive (fear of parental displeasure) disappears, and playing becomes necessary to the person's self-image.
sections.simple: Functional autonomy means adult motives become independent of the reasons they started, just as a grown tree no longer needs its seed. Perseverative functional autonomy covers low-level habits and addictions that continue without reward. Propriate functional autonomy covers motives tied to our self-image and values, such as continuing piano because we are good at it and it defines us.
keyPoints: Mature adults' motives are not functionally connected to the experiences in which they began.
Analogies: the tree and its seed; adults and their parents; working hard after financial security is reached.
Adult motives must be understood by why people act as they do today, not by childhood.
Perseverative level: addictions, routines; persists without reward; not integral to personality (maze-running rat).
Propriate level: tied to values, self-image and lifestyle; ego keeps motives that enhance self-esteem; we enjoy what we do well.

sections.heading: The Organizing of Our Propriate Functioning
sections.detailed:
Propriate functioning is an organising process that maintains our sense of self. It determines how we perceive the world, what we remember from experience and how our thoughts are directed. These perceptual and cognitive processes are selective: from the mass of stimuli around us they pick out only those relevant to our interests and values.

Allport said this organising process is governed by three principles (Review Question 7):

1. Organizing the energy level. This principle explains how we acquire new motives. New motives arise out of necessity, to use up surplus energy that might otherwise be expressed in destructive and harmful ways. For example, people who retire have extra time and energy that ideally should be directed into new interests and activities.

2. Mastery and competence. This principle concerns the level at which we choose to satisfy motives. Adequate achievement is not enough. Healthy, mature adults are motivated to perform better and more efficiently, to master new skills and to increase their competence.

3. Propriate patterning. This describes a striving for consistency and integration of the personality. We organise our perceptual and cognitive processes around the self, keeping what enhances self-image and rejecting the rest. Our propriate motives therefore depend on the structure or pattern of the self.

Limits of functional autonomy. Allport accepted that not all behaviour and motives can be explained by these principles. Some behaviours are not under the control of functionally autonomous motives: reflexes, fixations, neuroses and behaviours arising from biological drives. This qualification is consistent with his view that neurotic adults remain tied to childhood drives and that biological urges govern infancy.

Putting it together. Functional autonomy as a whole explains how adult motives free themselves from their origins; propriate functional autonomy explains which motives survive (those that serve the self); and the three principles explain how new motives arise (energy), the standard to which they are pursued (mastery), and how they are fitted into a consistent self (patterning).
sections.simple: Our sense of self organises what we notice, remember and think about. Three principles govern this: we take up new motives to use surplus energy, we strive for mastery rather than just adequacy, and we keep only what fits and enhances our self-image. Reflexes, fixations, neuroses and biological drives are not functionally autonomous.
keyPoints: Propriate functioning selectively organises perception, memory and thought around interests and values.
Organizing the energy level: new motives arise to absorb excess energy (e.g., after retirement).
Mastery and competence: mature adults seek to improve and master skills, not just be adequate.
Propriate patterning: striving for consistency; keep what enhances self-image, reject the rest.
Not functionally autonomous: reflexes, fixations, neuroses, biological drives.

sections.heading: Personality Development in Childhood: The Unique Self (the Proprium)
sections.detailed:
Allport used the term proprium for the self or ego. He deliberately avoided the words "self" and "ego" because other theorists had given them so many different meanings.

The word is best understood through the adjective "appropriate". The proprium includes those aspects of personality that are distinctive and therefore appropriate to our individual emotional life. These aspects are unique to each person and unite his or her attitudes, perceptions and intentions. In other words, the proprium is the core that makes a personality one's own and holds it together.

The proprium links many parts of Allport's theory. It is the source of propriate functional autonomy: the ego decides which motives to keep, retaining those that enhance self-esteem and self-image. It underlies the organising principles of propriate functioning, especially propriate patterning, by which perceptions and thoughts are organised around the self. And it develops gradually through childhood and adolescence in seven stages, which the next section describes.

Before the proprium. Allport stressed that the newborn has no proprium at all. The infant experiences no self-consciousness or self-awareness, and has not yet separated "me" from everything else. Sensory impressions from the environment are responded to automatically and reflexively, with no ego mediating between stimulus and response. Allport described infants as pleasure seeking, destructive, selfish, impatient and dependent, calling them "unsocialized horrors". They have little that could be called personality; they are simply driven by reflexes to reduce tension and maximise pleasure.

This picture of infancy fits Allport's idea of two discontinuous personalities: a biologically driven infant and a psychologically driven, conscious adult. The proprium is what bridges the gap, emerging stage by stage until adolescence, when propriate striving toward future goals completes it. Review Question 11 asks you to describe the proprium; include its meaning, why Allport chose the term, what it unites, and its absence in infancy.
sections.simple: The proprium is Allport's word for the self or ego, chosen to avoid confusion with other theorists' terms. It covers the distinctive parts of personality that unite our attitudes, perceptions and intentions. Newborns have no proprium; Allport called them 'unsocialized horrors' driven only by reflexes.
keyPoints: Proprium = Allport's term for the self or ego; he rejected 'self' and 'ego' because of their many meanings.
Understood via 'appropriate': the distinctive aspects appropriate to our emotional life.
Unique to each person; unites attitudes, perceptions and intentions.
Infants have no self-awareness; react reflexively, seek pleasure and reduce tension.
Allport called infants 'unsocialized horrors' with little personality.

sections.heading: Stages of Development of the Proprium
sections.detailed:
Allport described the development of the proprium in seven stages from infancy to adolescence (Table 7.1).

Stages 1-3 (birth to about age 3-4; the table says the first three years, the text says birth to about 4):
1. Bodily self. Infants become aware of a "bodily me", recognising their own existence and distinguishing their bodies from objects around them, for example telling apart their own fingers from the object they are holding.
2. Self-identity. Children sense continuity of identity: they remain the same person despite changes in body and abilities. Self-identity is strengthened when they learn their names and see themselves as distinct from others.
3. Self-esteem. Children discover they can accomplish things on their own and learn to take pride in this. They are motivated to build, explore and manipulate objects, which can sometimes be destructive. If parents frustrate the need to explore, emerging self-esteem may be thwarted and replaced by humiliation and anger.

Stages 4-5 (about ages 4-6):
4. Extension of self. Children become aware of the objects and people in their environment and identify them as belonging to them: "my house", "my parents", "my school".
5. Self-image. Children develop actual and ideal self-images, how they see themselves and how they would like to see themselves. These grow out of interaction with parents, who make children aware of their expectations and of how far the child is meeting or failing them.

Stage 6 (ages 6-12):
6. Self as a rational coper. Children realise that reason and logic can be applied to solving everyday problems.

Stage 7 (adolescence):
7. Propriate striving. Adolescents start to formulate long-range plans and goals for the future. Until they do, the proprium remains incomplete.

Adulthood. According to the table, normal mature adults are functionally autonomous and independent of childhood motives; they function rationally in the present and consciously create their own lifestyles.

Review Question 10 asks for the first three stages: bodily self, self-identity and self-esteem, with the changes in each. Notice the role of parents at stages 3 and 5, which connects to the importance of the infant-mother bond.
sections.simple: The proprium develops in seven stages: bodily self, self-identity and self-esteem (first few years); extension of self and self-image (4 to 6); self as a rational coper (6 to 12); and propriate striving (adolescence). Only when teenagers form future goals is the self complete.
keyPoints: Bodily self: awareness of one's body as separate from objects.
Self-identity: continuity of identity; learning one's name. Self-esteem: pride in accomplishment; parental frustration causes humiliation and anger.
Extension of self ('my house') and self-image (actual and ideal), ages 4-6.
Self as rational coper (6-12): using reason and logic for everyday problems.
Propriate striving (adolescence): long-range goals; the proprium is incomplete until then.

sections.heading: The Importance of the Infant-Mother Bond
sections.detailed:
Social interaction with parents is vitally important throughout all stages of proprium development, but the most important factor of all is the infant-mother bond as a source of affection and security.

When needs are met. If the mother or primary caregiver provides enough affection and security, the proprium develops gradually and steadily and the child achieves positive psychological growth. Childhood motives are then free to be transformed into the autonomous propriate strivings of adulthood. A pattern of personal dispositions forms, and the result is a mature, emotionally healthy adult. This answers Review Question 12: the parental behaviours necessary for positive growth are the provision of sufficient affection and security, especially by the mother or primary caregiver (and, from the stages, not frustrating the child's need to explore, and making expectations clear).

When needs are frustrated. If childhood needs are frustrated, the self does not mature properly. The child becomes insecure, aggressive, demanding, jealous and self-centred, and psychological growth is stunted. The outcome is a neurotic adult who functions at the level of childhood drives. Such an adult's motives do not become functionally autonomous; they stay tied to their original conditions. Traits and personal dispositions do not develop, and the personality remains undifferentiated, as it was in infancy.

How the theory explains emotional disturbance (Review Question 13). This is Allport's account of adult neurosis. Emotional disturbance is the result of failed proprium development caused by inadequate affection and security in childhood. The disturbed adult has not made the break from childhood that normal adults make; functional autonomy has not occurred. This is consistent with his earlier claims that the unconscious and the past matter only for neurotic people, that the abnormal personality functions at an infantile level, and that neuroses are among the behaviours not governed by functionally autonomous motives.

There is an interesting tension here worth noting in a 10-mark answer: Allport insists healthy adults are free of childhood, yet whether one becomes healthy depends heavily on childhood experience with the mother.
sections.simple: The bond with the mother, giving affection and security, is the most important influence on the developing self. If these needs are met, the child grows into a mature adult with functionally autonomous motives. If they are frustrated, the child becomes insecure and self-centred and grows into a neurotic adult still driven by childhood needs.
keyPoints: Parent interaction matters at every stage; the infant-mother bond matters most.
Sufficient affection and security lead to steady proprium growth and a healthy adult.
Frustrated needs make the child insecure, aggressive, demanding, jealous and self-centred.
Result: a neurotic adult functioning at the level of childhood drives; motives not functionally autonomous.
Personality stays undifferentiated, as in infancy.

sections.heading: The Healthy Adult Personality
sections.detailed:
For Allport, healthy personality development is a movement from a biologically dominated organism in infancy to a mature psychological organism in adulthood. Our motives become separated from childhood and oriented toward the future. If childhood needs for affection and security have been met, the proprium develops satisfactorily, and the adult personality grows out of childhood without being dominated or determined by childhood drives.

Allport described six criteria of the normal, mature, emotionally healthy adult personality:

1. Extension of the sense of self. Mature adults extend their sense of self beyond themselves to other people and activities.
2. Warm relating to others. They relate warmly to others, showing intimacy, compassion and tolerance.
3. Self-acceptance and emotional security. A high degree of self-acceptance helps them achieve emotional security.
4. Realistic perception, skills and work. They hold a realistic perception of life, develop personal skills, and make a commitment to some kind of work.
5. Humour and self-objectification. They have a sense of humour and self-objectification, meaning understanding of or insight into themselves.
6. A unifying philosophy of life. They subscribe to a unifying philosophy that directs the personality toward future goals.

Adults who meet these criteria can be described as emotionally healthy and functionally autonomous, independent of childhood motives. As a result they cope with the present and plan for the future without being victims of what happened in their early years.

Links to other parts of the chapter. Criterion 6 is connected to the Study of Values: Allport and his colleagues proposed that personal values form the basis of our unifying philosophy of life. Criterion 4's emphasis on skill and work echoes the principle of mastery and competence. Criterion 1 continues the childhood stage of extension of self. The chapter summary lists the characteristics slightly more finely (extension of self, warm relating, emotional security, realistic perception, development of skills, commitment to work, self-objectification, unifying philosophy), so in an exam it helps to name all of these.
sections.simple: Healthy adults have grown from biology-driven infants into psychologically mature people whose motives point to the future. Allport gave six signs: extending the self to others and activities, warm relationships, self-acceptance and emotional security, realistic perception with skills and work commitment, humour and self-insight, and a unifying philosophy of life.
keyPoints: Healthy growth: from biologically dominated infant to mature psychological adult.
Criteria 1-3: extension of self; warm relating (intimacy, compassion, tolerance); self-acceptance and emotional security.
Criterion 4: realistic perception, personal skills, commitment to work.
Criteria 5-6: humour and self-objectification; a unifying philosophy of life directing future goals.
Such adults are functionally autonomous and not victimised by their early years.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Optimism. Because emotionally healthy adults are not tied to childhood conflicts, Allport's theory presents an optimistic image of people in conscious control of their lives, dealing rationally with present situations, planning for the future and actively shaping an identity. We are always in a process of becoming, creatively designing and carrying out an appropriate lifestyle shaped more by present events and future plans than by the past.

Free will versus determinism. Allport took a moderate position. He allowed free choice in our deliberations about the future, but recognised that some behaviour is determined by traits and personal dispositions, which are hard to change once formed.

Nature versus nurture. Both heredity and environment influence personality. Genes supply basic physique, temperament and intelligence; these raw materials are shaped by learning and experience.

Uniqueness versus universality. Allport believed firmly in uniqueness. Common traits show some universality in behaviour, but individual traits or personal dispositions describe our nature more precisely.

The ultimate goal of life (Review Question 15). For Freud the goal was tension reduction. Allport took the opposite view: the ultimate and necessary goal of life is to increase tension, pushing us to keep seeking new sensations and challenges. Once one challenge is met, we seek another. The reward lies in the process of achieving rather than in the achievement itself, in striving for the goal rather than reaching it; in his words, getting there is more fun than being there. We constantly need new goals to motivate us and to maintain an optimal level of tension. We achieve this goal, then, by continually setting and pursuing new goals and challenges. The chapter summary adds that we grow through an inherent need for autonomy, individuality and selfhood.

Allport the person. His optimistic image of human nature matched his liberal personal stance and interest in social reform. The humanistic attitude of his work was mirrored in his personality: colleagues and students described him as someone who genuinely cared about people, and they returned that feeling.
sections.simple: Allport was optimistic: healthy adults consciously shape their lives and are always 'becoming'. He took a middle position on free will, gave weight to both heredity and environment, and stressed uniqueness. Unlike Freud, he said the goal of life is to increase tension by constantly seeking new challenges, because striving is the reward.
keyPoints: Optimistic view: conscious, rational adults always in the process of becoming.
Free will vs determinism: moderate; free choice about the future, but traits determine some behaviour.
Nature-nurture: genes give physique, temperament, intelligence; learning shapes them.
Uniqueness: personal dispositions describe us better than common traits.
Ultimate goal: increase (not reduce) tension; striving matters more than arriving.

sections.heading: Assessment in Allport's Theory
sections.detailed:
Allport wrote more about personality assessment than most other theorists. In Pattern and Growth in Personality (1961) he observed that although there were many approaches to assessment, no single technique was best. Personality is so complex that many techniques must be used to evaluate it.

He listed 11 major methods:
1. Constitutional and physiological diagnosis
2. Cultural setting, membership and role
3. Personal documents and case studies
4. Self-appraisal
5. Conduct analysis
6. Ratings
7. Tests and scales
8. Projective techniques
9. Depth analysis
10. Expressive behaviour
11. Synoptic procedures, which combine information from several sources into a synopsis

Of these, Allport relied most heavily on two: the personal-document technique and the Study of Values. He also observed expressive behaviour, which the chapter discusses under research.

It is worth noticing a tension with the research section: although projective techniques and depth analysis appear on his list, Allport elsewhere argued that projective tests such as the TAT and Rorschach may distort the picture of normal personality because they focus on unconscious forces that have little effect on healthy adults, and that case studies focus on the past. So listing a method did not mean he favoured it for studying healthy people; he preferred direct methods such as asking people to describe themselves, analysing their own documents, and measuring their values.

His multi-method position also reflects his balance between idiographic methods (personal documents, focused on the single case) and nomothetic ones (standardised tests such as the Study of Values, comparing large samples).
sections.simple: Allport believed personality is too complex for any single assessment method, so he listed 11 techniques. He relied mainly on the personal-document technique and the Study of Values, and also studied expressive behaviour.
keyPoints: Allport wrote more on assessment than most theorists; no single best technique exists.
Listed 11 methods in Pattern and Growth in Personality (1961).
Synoptic procedures combine information from several sources into a synopsis.
Relied most on the personal-document technique and the Study of Values.
Also observed expressive behaviour.

sections.heading: The Personal-Document Technique
sections.detailed:
The personal-document technique involves studying a person's written or spoken records, such as diaries, autobiographies, letters and literary compositions, to determine the number and kinds of personality traits the person has. It is an idiographic method because it focuses intensively on one individual.

Letters from Jenny. Allport's most famous case was his analysis of more than 300 letters written over a 12-year period by a middle-aged woman called Jenny (Allport, 1965, 1966). It was later revealed (Winter, 1993a) that Jenny was the mother of Allport's college roommate and had written the letters to Allport and his wife.

How the method works. A group of judges reads the autobiographical or biographical material and records the traits they find. If the judges agree reasonably well, their assessments can be grouped into a relatively small number of categories. In the Jenny study, 36 judges listed nearly 200 traits. Because many of the terms were synonyms, Allport reduced them to eight categories.

Computer analysis. One of Allport's students, Paige (1966), carried out a computer analysis of the letters, searching for categories of words that might indicate a particular trait. For example, words expressing anger, rage, hostility and aggression were coded as the trait of aggression. This approach is more sophisticated and quantitative than Allport's original analysis because it involves fewer subjective judgments. The computer analysis produced eight prominent traits that were similar to the categories Allport had found.

Conclusion. Because of this agreement, Allport concluded that his subjective approach to assessment provided valid information about traits, comparable to the more objective computer method. The Reflections section adds that interest in the personal-document technique has recently revived (Barenbaum, 2008; Zunshine, 2010).
sections.simple: The personal-document technique studies a person's diaries, letters and other writings to find their traits. Allport analysed over 300 letters from 'Jenny': 36 judges found about 200 traits, which he reduced to eight. A later computer analysis by Paige found eight similar traits, supporting Allport's subjective method.
keyPoints: Examines diaries, autobiographies, letters, compositions and other written or spoken records.
Jenny: 300+ letters over 12 years; she was the mother of Allport's college roommate (Winter, 1993a).
36 judges listed nearly 200 traits, reduced to eight categories.
Paige (1966) computer word-category analysis also found eight similar traits.
Agreement suggested Allport's subjective method was valid.

sections.heading: The Study of Values
sections.detailed:
Allport and two colleagues developed an objective self-report test called the Study of Values (Allport, Vernon & Lindzey, 1960). They proposed that our personal values form the basis of our unifying philosophy of life, which is one of the six criteria of a mature, healthy personality.

Values are personality traits that represent strongly held interests and motivations. Allport believed everyone has some degree of each type of value, but one or two will be dominant in a given personality. The six categories are:

1. Theoretical values: concerned with discovering truth; marked by an empirical, intellectual and rational approach to life.
2. Economic values: concerned with what is useful and practical.
3. Aesthetic values: relate to artistic experiences and to form, harmony and grace.
4. Social values: reflect human relationships, altruism and philanthropy.
5. Political values: concern personal power, influence and prestige in all endeavours, not only in politics.
6. Religious values: concerned with the mystical and with understanding the universe as a whole.

Methodological significance. The Study of Values is a nomothetic instrument: it is a standardised psychological test that allows statistical comparison of large samples. This shows that although Allport favoured the idiographic study of individual cases, he also used nomothetic methods where he considered them appropriate. It also illustrates his view that simply asking people about themselves is a more reliable way to learn about healthy personalities than projective tests.

Exam tip. A common question pairs the personal-document technique (idiographic, subjective judges plus computer check) with the Study of Values (objective, self-report, six values, linked to the unifying philosophy of life). Remember that the political value is about power in all areas of life, not just politics, a frequent MCQ trap.
sections.simple: The Study of Values is a self-report test by Allport, Vernon and Lindzey that measures six values: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political and religious. Everyone has some of each, but one or two dominate. Values form the basis of a person's unifying philosophy of life.
keyPoints: Objective self-report test (Allport, Vernon & Lindzey, 1960).
Values are the basis of the unifying philosophy of life, a maturity criterion.
Values are traits representing strongly held interests and motivations; one or two dominate.
Six values: theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political, religious.
Political values concern power, influence and prestige in all endeavours; the test is nomothetic.

sections.heading: Research on Allport's Theory
sections.detailed:
Allport's views on method. Allport criticised psychologists who insisted that experimental and correlational methods were the only legitimate ways to study personality. Not every aspect of personality can be tested in those ways, he argued, and psychologists should be more open and eclectic in their methods.

Against clinical methods for healthy people. He also opposed applying methods designed for emotionally disturbed people to the study of healthy people. Case studies focus on the past, so he thought them of no value for understanding normal adults, whose personality is divorced from childhood influences. Projective techniques such as the Thematic Apperception Test and the Rorschach inkblot test may distort the picture of normal personality because they deal with unconscious forces that have little effect on healthy adults. Allport suggested that more reliable information could be obtained simply by asking people to describe themselves, which reveals their dominant traits.

Idiographic versus nomothetic. Allport favoured the idiographic approach, the study of the individual case, as shown by his use of personal documents. But he also used nomothetic methods, involving statistical analysis of differences among large samples, when he thought them appropriate. Psychological tests like the Study of Values are nomothetic.

This preference had consequences. As the Reflections section explains, Allport's idiographic approach ran against the dominant nomothetic trend in psychology, and his theory as a whole has stimulated little direct research. The area where considerable research has been done is expressive behaviour, described in the following sections. That research, much of it by later investigators, examines how facial expressions, voice, gestures and other spontaneous behaviours reveal personality and emotion, and how this varies with gender, age, experience, emotional state and culture.
sections.simple: Allport thought experimental and correlational methods were too narrow and wanted psychologists to be more open. He rejected case studies and projective tests for healthy people, preferring to ask people to describe themselves. He mainly used idiographic (single-case) methods but also nomothetic tests like the Study of Values.
keyPoints: Experimental and correlational methods are not the only legitimate ways to study personality; be eclectic.
Case studies focus on the past and are of no value for normal adults.
Projective tests (TAT, Rorschach) may distort normal personality by focusing on the unconscious.
Asking people to describe themselves reveals dominant traits more reliably.
Favoured idiographic study but used nomothetic methods (e.g., Study of Values) when appropriate.

sections.heading: Expressive Behavior: Nature, Gender and Age, and Interpreting Facial Expressions
sections.detailed:
Expressive versus coping behaviour. Allport did considerable research on expressive behaviour, behaviour that expresses our personality traits. He contrasted it with coping behaviour, which is purposeful, consciously planned and carried out, determined by needs arising from the situation and usually aimed at changing the environment. Expressive behaviour is spontaneous and reflects basic aspects of personality; it is hard to change, has no specific purpose and is usually displayed without awareness.

Allport's example is public speaking. A speaker communicates on two levels. The formal, planned level (coping) is the content of the lecture. The informal, unplanned level (expressive) is the speaker's movements, gestures and vocal inflections: nervousness, talking fast, pacing or fidgeting with an earring. These spontaneous behaviours can reveal the speaker's personality.

Allport's landmark study. Allport and Vernon (1933) gave subjects various tasks and judged the consistency of their expressive movements across situations. They found high consistency in voice, handwriting, posture and gestures, and from these inferred traits such as introversion and extraversion.

Later research. Much work has examined facial and vocal expression (Russell, Bachorowski & Fernandez-Dols, 2003). Personality can be assessed from voice recordings, films, videotapes and even still photographs; facial expressions, vocal inflections and idiosyncratic gestures can reveal traits to trained observers (e.g., Allport & Cantril, 1934; Berry, 1990; DePaulo, 1993; Riggio & Friedman, 1986). Some people form reliable impressions of a stranger's personality from facial appearance and expression alone (Berry & Wero, 1993); observers accurately judged anxiety after watching a film of a person for no more than 30 seconds (Ambody & Rosenthal, 1992).

Effects of gender and age. Women and younger people recognise emotions in facial expressions better than men and older people (Sasson et al., 2010). Children can read facial expressions accurately as early as age 5, improving rapidly afterwards (Gao & Maurer, 2010). Yearbook photos showed that women graduates with positive expressions at 21 reported greater subjective well-being at 27, 43 and 52, better marriages, and higher affiliation, competence and achievement orientation (Harker & Keltner, 2001).

Interpreting facial expressions. Experience shapes recognition. Physically abused 8- to 10-year-olds identified anger in adult female faces more readily than non-abused controls (Pollak & Sinha, 2002). Adults with major depression needed more intense expressions to recognise happiness but less intense ones to recognise sadness (Joormann & Gotlib, 2006). Socially anxious children were better at interpreting expressions, and depressed adults better at recognising sad faces (Ale et al., 2010; Gollan et al., 2010). Japanese children who played more video games recognised expressions better (Tamamiya & Jiraki, 2013). Close friends decode sadness, anger and happiness far more accurately than casual acquaintances (Zhang & Parmley, 2011). Such findings strongly support Allport's claim that expressive behaviour reflects personality traits.
sections.simple: Expressive behaviour is spontaneous, unplanned and reveals personality (a speaker's fidgeting); coping behaviour is planned and purposeful (the speech content). Allport and Vernon found people's voice, handwriting, posture and gestures were consistent. Later studies show personality can be read from faces, that women, young people and close friends read emotions better, and that experiences like abuse or depression change what we notice.
keyPoints: Expressive behaviour: spontaneous, purposeless, hard to change, outside awareness; coping behaviour: planned, purposeful, aimed at change.
Allport & Vernon (1933): high consistency in voice, handwriting, posture and gestures.
Personality can be judged from voice, film, video and still photos; anxiety judged in 30 seconds (Ambody & Rosenthal).
Women and younger people read faces better; children from age 5; positive yearbook smiles predicted later well-being.
Abuse, depression, social anxiety, video gaming and close friendship affect recognition of emotions.

sections.heading: Coding Facial Expressions and Emotional States
sections.detailed:
Coding facial expressions. A long-term research programme by Paul Ekman identified facial expressions of seven emotions that can be objectively and consistently distinguished: anger, contempt, disgust, fear, sadness, surprise and happiness (Ekman, Matsumoto & Friesen, 1997). Ekman, director of the Human Interaction Laboratory at the University of California at San Francisco, and colleagues developed a coding system based on 43 facial muscles, giving 3,000 different configurations for reading emotional expressions.

This Facial Action Coding System (FACS) is used in the US by police departments, the CIA and the FBI to detect lying by criminal suspects and terrorists, on the principle that tiny movements of facial muscles give them away (Kaufman, 2002). In 2009 Time magazine named Ekman one of the world's 100 most influential people (Taylor, 2009).

Personality factors in the face. Other research shows that basic aspects of personality appear in facial expressions (Keltner, 1997):
- Neuroticism shows in looks of anger, contempt and fear.
- Agreeableness shows in laughter and other friendly social expressions.
- Extraversion shows in smiles, laughter and other expressions of enjoyment and amusement.
- Conscientiousness shows in expressions of embarrassment: a tightly controlled smile, averted gaze, and head movements down and away from the observer.

Recognising smiles. We recognise smiles by unconsciously mimicking them. Using the same muscles as the smiling person activates the same brain regions that are active in that person (Niedenthal et al., 2010; Zimmer, 2011).

Emotional states and facial expressions. Type A behaviour, a pattern suggested to be linked to the potential for heart disease, has been distinguished from Type B by expressions of disgust, glaring, grimacing and scowling (Chesney et al., 1997). Among depressed patients in Switzerland, facial expressions distinguished those who later attempted suicide from those who did not (Heller & Haynal, 1997). Japanese college students high in anxiety showed different facial expressions, especially around the mouth and the left side of the face, from those low in anxiety (Nakamura, 2002). The chapter concludes that these results confirm Allport's ideas.
sections.simple: Paul Ekman identified seven distinguishable facial emotions and built the Facial Action Coding System from 43 face muscles, used by police, the CIA and FBI to detect lies. Personality traits such as neuroticism, agreeableness, extraversion and conscientiousness each show in typical expressions. Facial expressions also distinguish Type A people, suicide risk among depressed patients, and high anxiety.
keyPoints: Ekman: seven emotions (anger, contempt, disgust, fear, sadness, surprise, happiness).
FACS: 43 facial muscles, 3,000 configurations; used to detect lying.
Keltner (1997): neuroticism, agreeableness, extraversion and conscientiousness each show in distinct expressions.
We recognise smiles by unconscious mimicry.
Facial expressions distinguish Type A from Type B, later suicide attempters, and high-anxiety students.

sections.heading: Cultural Differences in Facial Expressions
sections.detailed:
Are facial expressions universal or do they vary across cultures (Review Question 17)? The chapter presents evidence on both sides.

Evidence for universality. Studies of American and Chinese infants and adults found that some basic emotions were shown by identical facial expressions in both cultures and both age groups (Albright et al., 1997; Camras et al., 1998).

Evidence for cultural differences.
- Comparing American, Chinese and Japanese infants, Chinese infants showed consistently less variety in facial expression. American infants differed significantly from Chinese infants but not so much from Japanese infants (Camras, 1998).
- Facial expressions of emotion in a remote tribe in northwestern Namibia did not match those of American subjects, suggesting that perceptions of emotion are not universal (Gendron et al., 2014).
- Among 3-year-old girls, White children smiled more than mainland Chinese or Chinese-American children. Maternal strictness and the number of other children and adults in the home also influenced intensity, so expressiveness varied with both cultural and family characteristics (Camras et al., 2006).
- Adults in the US and Japan were each much better at recognising expressions of people from their own culture (Dailey et al., 2010); the same East-West difference appeared when faces were shown on robots (Trovato et al., 2014).
- When faces were digitised to be emotionally neutral, White faces were judged angry more often than Black faces, and Black faces were judged happy or surprised more often (Zebrowitz, Kikuchi & Fellous, 2010).
- Eastern and Western cultures differ consistently in recognising emotions and even in how faces change: Easterners express emotion mainly with the eyes, Westerners with the eyebrows and mouth (Jack, Caldara & Schyns, 2012).
- People in Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan showed less intense expressions in Facebook pictures than Americans (Huang & Park, 2013).
- Among people high in depression watching a humorous film, Caucasian Americans showed fewer smiles and facial reactions than Asian Americans (Chentsova-Dutton, Tsai & Gotlib, 2010).

Conclusion. Some basic emotions appear to be expressed similarly across cultures, but the variety, intensity, facial regions used and accuracy of recognition differ with culture and family background. The chapter summary puts it cautiously: some research suggests consistency across cultures, while many studies show differences.
sections.simple: Some basic emotions look the same on American and Chinese faces. But many studies find differences: Chinese infants show less variety, a Namibian tribe's expressions did not match Americans', people recognise their own culture's faces better, Easterners use the eyes while Westerners use eyebrows and mouth, and Asian Facebook photos are less intense.
keyPoints: Universality: identical expressions of basic emotions in American and Chinese infants and adults.
Chinese infants less varied than American and Japanese infants (Camras, 1998).
Namibian tribe's expressions did not match Americans', suggesting perceptions of emotion are not universal.
Own-culture advantage in recognition (US and Japan), even with robot faces.
East uses eyes, West uses eyebrows and mouth; Asians show less intense expressions online.

sections.heading: Computer Recognition of Facial Expressions
sections.detailed:
Recognition by computers. If people can accurately interpret facial expressions, can computers? Apparently yes. A computer program was developed that monitors video images of faces at 30 frames per second. It achieved a high degree of accuracy in recognising basic emotions, including happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, anger and surprise (Susskind, Littlewort, Bartlett, Movellan & Anderson, 2007).

Transmitting emotion through computers. A further question is whether computers can be used to transmit emotional states. A study of adolescents in the Netherlands (average age 16) used emoticons to study the online communication of feelings. In simulated chat rooms, the teenagers used more emoticons in a social context than in a task- or job-oriented context. They used more positive emoticons (such as smiles) in positive situations and more negative emoticons (such as sad faces) in negative situations, just as people do face to face. The researchers concluded that people express emotions in computer-mediated communication in a similar way to face-to-face situations (Derks, Bos & von Grumbkow, 2007).

Review Question 18 asks how people express emotions in computer-mediated communication: through emoticons, used more in social than task contexts and matched to the emotional tone of the situation, mirroring face-to-face expression. The second part of the question (how you express your own emotions online) is personal; a good answer relates one's own use of emojis or similar cues to these findings.

Highlights box. The chapter summarises research on expressive behaviour as showing that: personality traits can be assessed from facial expressions; women and children are better than men and older people at reading expressions; close friends decode emotion better than strangers; as many as seven separate emotions can be identified in the face; we recognise smiles by unconscious mimicry; depressed people are better at recognising sad expressions; and computers can recognise and express basic emotions.
sections.simple: A computer program reading video at 30 frames per second recognised basic emotions very accurately. Dutch teenagers in chat rooms used emoticons much like real facial expressions: more in social chats, happy icons in positive situations and sad ones in negative situations. So people express emotions online much as they do face to face.
keyPoints: Program monitoring faces at 30 frames per second accurately recognised six basic emotions (Susskind et al., 2007).
Dutch adolescents (average age 16) used more emoticons in social than task-oriented chats.
Positive emoticons in positive situations, negative in negative situations.
Emotions are expressed online much as in face-to-face contact (Derks et al., 2007).
Highlights: traits readable from faces; seven emotions; mimicry of smiles; computers recognise emotions.

sections.heading: Reflections on Allport's Theory
sections.detailed:
Limited research. Although expressive behaviour has been researched extensively, Allport's theory as a whole has stimulated little research testing its propositions. His idiographic approach ran against the main current of contemporary psychology, which favoured nomothetic research, the study of large groups using sophisticated statistics. His focus on emotionally healthy adults also conflicted with clinical psychology of the time, which dealt with neurotic and psychotic people.

Questions and criticisms.
- Testability: it is difficult to translate Allport's concepts into specific propositions testable by the experimental method. How can functional autonomy or propriate striving be observed or manipulated in a laboratory?
- Functional autonomy: Allport did not explain how an original motive is transformed into an autonomous one. Once a person is financially secure, by what process does working for money become working for its own sake? Without an explained mechanism, we cannot predict which childhood motives will become autonomous.
- Uniqueness: his focus on the individual is so exclusive that generalising from one person to another becomes impossible.
- Discontinuity: many psychologists reject his proposed breaks between child and adult, animal and human, and normal and abnormal, pointing out that research on children, animals and disturbed people has produced considerable knowledge about healthy adults.

Recognition and influence. Despite these criticisms, many psychologists still believe Allport's views offer a better basis for understanding personality than most other theories (Piekkola, 2011). His approach to development, his emphasis on uniqueness and his focus on goals are reflected in the humanistic psychologists Abraham Maslow and Carl Rogers. He is often regarded as one of the first psychologists to bring humanistic values into the field (Jeshmaridian, 2007). Interest in his work has revived with the current focus on personality traits, which provides empirical support for some of his ideas. His work on the expression of emotion has been vitally important to the development of cognitive neuroscience, and interest in the personal-document technique has revived (Barenbaum, 2008; Zunshine, 2010).

His books are readable and his concepts have commonsense appeal. His emphasis on conscious, rational determinants offers an alternative to the psychoanalytic picture of people driven by irrational, unconscious forces, and his view that people are shaped more by future expectations than past events suits a hopeful, humanistic philosophy. His most enduring contributions are making personality study academically respectable and emphasising genetic factors within a trait approach.
sections.simple: Apart from expressive behaviour, Allport's theory has produced little research, partly because his single-case approach went against mainstream psychology. Critics say functional autonomy is hard to test and its mechanism unexplained, his uniqueness focus prevents generalising, and his child-adult and normal-abnormal splits are doubtful. Still, he influenced Maslow and Rogers, helped found humanistic psychology and made personality a respectable academic field.
keyPoints: Theory as a whole stimulated little research; idiographic approach ran counter to nomothetic mainstream.
Concepts like functional autonomy and propriate striving are hard to test experimentally.
Mechanism of transforming motives into autonomous ones is unexplained, so prediction is impossible.
Uniqueness prevents generalisation; discontinuity between child/adult, animal/human, normal/abnormal is disputed.
Influenced Maslow and Rogers; early humanistic voice; revived interest via trait research; made personality academically respectable.

The dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine characteristic behaviour and thought.
