In Allport's definition, personality is made of mind and body functioning together as a unit, neither purely mental nor purely biological.
Allport's view that there is no continuum between childhood and adult personality: infants are driven by biological urges, adults function psychologically.

To Allport, distinguishing characteristics that guide behaviour; consistent, enduring predispositions to respond similarly to different stimuli, measured on a continuum and subject to social, environmental and cultural influences.
Allport's original term for traits unique to a person that define his or her character; later renamed personal dispositions.
Traits shared by a number of people, such as members of a culture; they differ across cultures and change with social standards. Later simply called traits.
Traits peculiar to an individual, as opposed to traits shared by many people.
The most pervasive and powerful traits; a 'ruling passion' that touches almost every aspect of a person's life (e.g., sadism, chauvinism). Not everyone has one.
The handful (about 5 to 10) of outstanding traits that describe a person's behaviour, e.g., aggressiveness, self-pity, cynicism.
The least important traits, displayed inconspicuously and inconsistently, e.g., a minor preference for a type of music or food.
The idea that motives in the normal, mature adult are independent of the childhood experiences in which they originally appeared.
The level of functional autonomy relating to low-level and routine behaviours, such as addictions and habitual actions, that continue without external reward.
The level of functional autonomy relating to our values, self-image and lifestyle; the more important level for understanding adult motivation.

studies.title: Kaufman & Bristol (2001): anecdotes in teaching
studies.finding: Using personal anecdotes like the Allport-Freud story made lectures more enjoyable, and students learned and remembered information better in a social and personal context.

studies.title: Allport (1922): doctoral dissertation
studies.finding: An Experimental Study of the Traits of Personality was the first research on personality traits ever conducted in the United States.

studies.title: Allport (1965, 1966): Letters from Jenny
studies.finding: 36 judges reading 300+ letters written over 12 years listed nearly 200 traits, which Allport reduced to eight categories.

studies.title: Paige (1966): computer analysis of Jenny's letters
studies.finding: Coding word categories (e.g., anger, rage, hostility = aggression) yielded eight prominent traits similar to Allport's, supporting the validity of his subjective method.

studies.title: Allport & Vernon (1933): consistency of expressive movements
studies.finding: Across varied tasks, subjects showed high consistency in voice, handwriting, posture and gestures, from which traits such as introversion and extraversion were inferred.

studies.title: Expressive cues research (Russell et al., 2003; Allport & Cantril, 1934; Berry, 1990 and others)
studies.finding: Personality can be assessed from voice recordings, films, videotapes and even still photographs by trained observers.

studies.title: Berry & Wero (1993): impressions from faces
studies.finding: Some people form reliable impressions of a stranger's personality from facial appearance and expression alone.

studies.title: Ambody & Rosenthal (1992): thin slices
studies.finding: Observers accurately assessed anxiety from a film of a person lasting no more than 30 seconds.

studies.title: Sasson et al. (2010): gender and age
studies.finding: Women and younger people recognise emotions in facial expressions better than men and older people.

studies.title: Gao & Maurer (2010): children
studies.finding: Children can read facial expressions accurately as early as age 5, improving rapidly thereafter.

studies.title: Harker & Keltner (2001): yearbook photos
studies.finding: Women showing positive expressions at 21 had higher subjective well-being at 27, 43 and 52, better marriages, and higher affiliation, competence and achievement orientation.

studies.title: Pollak & Sinha (2002): abused children
studies.finding: Physically abused 8- to 10-year-olds identified anger in adult female faces more readily than non-abused controls.

studies.title: Joormann & Gotlib (2006): depression
studies.finding: Adults with major depression needed more intense expressions to identify happiness but less intense ones to identify sadness.

studies.title: Ale et al. (2010); Gollan et al. (2010): anxiety and depression
studies.finding: Socially anxious children were better at interpreting facial expressions; depressed adults were better at recognising sad expressions.

studies.title: Tamamiya & Jiraki (2013): video games
studies.finding: Japanese children who played more video games recognised facial expressions better.

studies.title: Zhang & Parmley (2011): friends vs acquaintances
studies.finding: Close friends decode sadness, anger and happiness far more accurately than casual acquaintances.

studies.title: Ekman, Matsumoto & Friesen (1997): seven emotions
studies.finding: Facial expressions of anger, contempt, disgust, fear, sadness, surprise and happiness can be objectively and consistently distinguished.

studies.title: Kaufman (2002): FACS and lie detection
studies.finding: The FACS (43 muscles, 3,000 configurations) is used by police, the CIA and FBI; tiny facial muscle movements betray lying suspects and terrorists.

studies.title: Keltner (1997): personality in the face
studies.finding: Neuroticism shows in anger, contempt and fear; agreeableness in laughter; extraversion in smiles and amusement; conscientiousness in embarrassment (controlled smile, averted gaze, head down and away).

studies.title: Niedenthal et al. (2010); Zimmer (2011): smile mimicry
studies.finding: We recognise smiles by unconsciously mimicking them, activating the same brain regions as the smiling person.

studies.title: Chesney et al. (1997): Type A
studies.finding: Type A behaviour was distinguished from Type B by expressions of disgust, glaring, grimacing and scowling.

studies.title: Heller & Haynal (1997): suicide risk
studies.finding: Among depressed patients in Switzerland, facial expressions distinguished those who later attempted suicide from those who did not.

studies.title: Nakamura (2002): anxiety
studies.finding: Highly anxious Japanese college students showed different facial expressions, especially around the mouth and left side of the face, than low-anxiety students.

studies.title: Albright et al. (1997); Camras et al. (1998): universality
studies.finding: Some basic emotions were shown by identical facial expressions in American and Chinese infants and adults.

studies.title: Camras (1998): three cultures
studies.finding: Chinese infants showed less variety of facial expression than American and Japanese infants; Americans differed significantly from Chinese but less from Japanese.

studies.title: Gendron et al. (2014): Namibian tribe
studies.finding: Facial expressions of emotion in a remote northwestern Namibian tribe did not match Americans', suggesting perceptions of emotion are not universal.

studies.title: Camras et al. (2006): 3-year-old girls
studies.finding: White girls smiled more than mainland Chinese or Chinese-American girls; maternal strictness and household size also affected intensity.

studies.title: Dailey et al. (2010); Trovato et al. (2014): own-culture advantage
studies.finding: US and Japanese adults recognised expressions of their own culture better; the same East-West difference appeared with robot faces.

studies.title: Zebrowitz, Kikuchi & Fellous (2010): neutral faces
studies.finding: Neutral White faces were judged angry more often than Black faces; Black faces were judged happy or surprised more often.

studies.title: Jack, Caldara & Schyns (2012): eyes vs mouth
studies.finding: Eastern cultures expressed emotion mainly with the eyes; Western cultures used eyebrows and mouth.

studies.title: Huang & Park (2013): Facebook pictures
studies.finding: People in Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan showed less intense facial expressions in Facebook photos than Americans.

studies.title: Chentsova-Dutton, Tsai & Gotlib (2010): depression and culture
studies.finding: Depressed Caucasian Americans showed fewer smiles and facial reactions to a humorous film than depressed Asian Americans.

studies.title: Susskind et al. (2007): computer recognition
studies.finding: A program monitoring faces at 30 frames per second recognised happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, anger and surprise with high accuracy.

studies.title: Derks, Bos & von Grumbkow (2007): emoticons
studies.finding: Dutch adolescents used more emoticons in social than task contexts, positive ones in positive and negative ones in negative situations, as in face-to-face contact.

examples.title: Functional autonomy: the gym habit
examples.text: A college student starts going to the gym only to impress classmates. Years later, nobody is watching, yet she trains daily because fitness has become part of who she is. The original motive vanished; the behaviour became an end in itself, propriate functional autonomy.

examples.title: Perseverative functional autonomy: checking the phone
examples.text: Someone keeps unlocking their phone every few minutes even when no notification has come. The habit once served a purpose but now runs on its own without reward, too low-level to be central to personality.

examples.title: Cardinal, central, secondary traits in a cricket captain
examples.text: A captain whose entire life revolves around winning shows something close to a cardinal trait. His central traits might be discipline, competitiveness and loyalty, the words a coach would put in a reference letter. Liking masala chai over coffee is a secondary trait only close friends would notice.

examples.title: Coping vs expressive behaviour in a viva
examples.text: In a viva, the planned answer you give about Allport is coping behaviour. Your shaking hands, quick speech and habit of tapping the desk are expressive behaviour, spontaneous and revealing of your personality.

examples.title: Extension of self and self-image in a child
examples.text: A five-year-old insists 'that's MY cycle' and 'my school is the best' (extension of self), and also wants to be 'a good boy like Papa says' (ideal self-image shaped by parental expectations).

practice.answer: Functional autonomy is Allport's idea that the motives of mature, emotionally healthy adults are independent of the childhood or earlier experiences in which they first appeared. Like a grown tree that no longer needs its seed, a motive that began as a means to an end (e.g., working for money) can become an end in itself.

Proprium is Allport's term for the ego or self, chosen because 'self' and 'ego' had too many meanings. Understood through the word 'appropriate', it covers the distinctive aspects of personality that are unique to each person and unite his or her attitudes, perceptions and intentions. It develops in seven stages from infancy to adolescence.

practice.q: Distinguish expressive behavior from coping behavior.
practice.answer: Coping behavior is consciously planned, purposeful and determined by the needs of a situation, usually aimed at changing the environment (e.g., the content of a speech). Expressive behavior is spontaneous, seemingly purposeless, hard to change and usually outside awareness, and it reveals personality traits (e.g., a speaker's gestures and fidgeting).

practice.q: What is the role of cognitive processes in personality, according to Allport?
practice.answer: Cognitive processes, meaning our conscious plans and intentions, are a vital part of personality. Allport criticised Freud for stressing unconscious, irrational forces. For him, deliberate intentions, what we want and strive for, are the keys to understanding behaviour, so the present is explained by the future rather than the past.

practice.q: What is Allport's ultimate and necessary goal of life, and how is it achieved?
practice.answer: Unlike Freud's tension reduction, Allport said the goal of life is to increase tension, pushing us to seek new sensations and challenges. We achieve it by continually setting new goals: once one challenge is met we seek another, because the reward lies in striving, not arriving ('getting there is more fun than being there').

practice.q: What problems in Allport's childhood and adolescence may have influenced his approach to personality?
practice.answer:
Allport was the youngest of four sons in Montezuma, Indiana. His home was dominated by a devout, strict mother who banned smoking, drinking, dancing, cards, bright colours and jewellery. He was too young to play with his brothers and isolated from other children; he felt rejected by his more 'masculine' brothers, suffered on the playground, and was good with words but poor at sports.

These conditions produced inferiority feelings, which he tried to offset by striving to excel. He described an identity quest. He identified with and envied his eldest brother Floyd, following him to Harvard and into a psychology Ph.D., and even as a successful psychologist felt in Floyd's shadow. At Harvard, social service gave him a sense of competence that offset his inferiority and helped his search for identity.

Influence on his theory: emulating Floyd may have threatened his sense of identity, so he may have asserted his individuality by claiming that adult motives are independent of childhood feelings, the core of functional autonomy. His emphasis on uniqueness also fits this need to be his own person. Finally, his traumatic meeting with Freud, who suggested Allport was the dirt-fearing boy in his story, convinced him that psychoanalysis digs too deep and that psychology should study conscious, visible motives. Ironically, his theory holds that healthy adults are unaffected by childhood, and he revealed little about his own.

practice.q: Explain Allport's definition of personality. How do heredity and environment influence personality in his system?
practice.answer:
After reviewing about 50 definitions, Allport (1961) defined personality as the dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine characteristic behaviour and thought. 'Dynamic organization' means personality constantly changes and grows, but in an organised way. 'Psychophysical' means mind and body work together as a unit; personality is neither purely mental nor purely biological. 'Determine' means all facets of personality activate or direct specific behaviours and thoughts. 'Characteristic behaviour and thought' means everything we do and think is typical of us, so each person is unique.

Heredity and environment: personality reflects both. Heredity provides raw materials such as physique, intelligence and temperament, which the environment then shapes, expands or limits. Thus both genetics and learning matter. But genes account for the major portion of our uniqueness, because the possible gene combinations are infinite and, except for identical twins, no one duplicates another's endowment. Genes interact with the social environment, and no two people, not even siblings in the same house, share exactly the same environment. The result is inevitably a unique personality, which is why Allport insisted psychology should study the individual case rather than group averages.

practice.q: Describe the characteristics of traits according to Allport, and distinguish individual from common traits.
practice.answer:
Allport defined traits as predispositions to respond in the same or a similar way to different kinds of stimuli: consistent, enduring ways of reacting to the environment. He listed five characteristics (Allport, 1937):

1. Traits are real and exist within each person; they are not invented labels or constructs.
2. Traits determine or cause behaviour; they motivate us to seek appropriate stimuli and interact with the environment to produce behaviour.
3. Traits can be demonstrated empirically, by inferring them from the consistency of responses observed over time.
4. Traits are interrelated and may overlap, e.g., aggressiveness and hostility often occur together.
5. Traits vary with the situation; a person may be neat in one setting and disorderly in another.

Individual versus common traits: individual traits are unique to a person and define his or her character. Common traits are shared by many people, such as members of a culture; people in different cultures therefore have different common traits, and common traits change as social standards and values change, showing they are subject to social, environmental and cultural influences. To avoid confusion Allport later renamed common traits simply 'traits' and individual traits 'personal dispositions'.

practice.q: How do cardinal, central and secondary traits differ? Which exerts the most powerful influence on personality?
practice.answer:
Allport's personal dispositions (traits peculiar to the individual) differ in intensity and significance, forming three levels.

Cardinal traits are so pervasive and influential that they touch almost every aspect of a person's life. Allport called a cardinal trait a 'ruling passion', a powerful force dominating behaviour, with examples such as sadism and chauvinism. Not everyone has a ruling passion, and those who do may not show it in every situation.

Central traits are the 5 to 10 themes that best describe a person's behaviour, and everyone has them. Allport's examples were aggressiveness, self-pity and cynicism. They are the qualities we mention when describing a friend or writing a letter of recommendation.

Secondary traits are the least influential. They appear much less consistently and may be so weak or inconspicuous that only a close friend notices them, e.g., a minor preference for a certain type of music or food.

The three differ in pervasiveness, consistency and visibility: cardinal (dominant, rare), central (characteristic, universal), secondary (peripheral, inconsistent). Cardinal traits exert the most powerful influence on personality, because they dominate behaviour across nearly all areas of life.

practice.q: Describe the first three stages of the development of the proprium and the role of parents in its development.
practice.answer:
Before the proprium appears, infants have no self-awareness and do not separate 'me' from the world. They react reflexively to reduce tension and maximise pleasure; Allport called them 'unsocialized horrors'. The first three stages emerge in roughly the first three to four years.

1. Bodily self: infants become aware of a 'bodily me', recognising their own existence and distinguishing their bodies from objects, such as their fingers from the object they grasp.
2. Self-identity: children realise their identity stays continuous despite changes in body and abilities. Learning their names and seeing themselves as distinct from others strengthens this.
3. Self-esteem: children discover they can do things on their own and take pride in it. They want to build, explore and manipulate objects, which may be destructive.

Role of parents: social interaction with parents matters at every stage. At the self-esteem stage, if parents frustrate the need to explore, self-esteem can be replaced by humiliation and anger. At the self-image stage, parents' expectations shape actual and ideal self-images. Most important is the infant-mother bond: sufficient affection and security from the mother or primary caregiver lets the proprium develop steadily and leads to a healthy adult; frustrated needs produce an insecure, aggressive, jealous child and later a neurotic adult functioning at the level of childhood drives.

practice.q: Describe the personal-document technique and the Study of Values as methods of assessment.
practice.answer:
Allport believed no single assessment technique is best and listed 11 methods, but relied most on these two.

Personal-document technique: the examination of diaries, autobiographies, letters, literary compositions and other written or spoken records to determine the number and kinds of a person's traits. Judges read the material and record traits; with reasonable agreement these are grouped into a few categories. In his famous case, more than 300 letters written over 12 years by 'Jenny' (later revealed by Winter to be his college roommate's mother), 36 judges listed nearly 200 traits, which Allport reduced to eight. His student Paige (1966) analysed the letters by computer, coding word categories (e.g., anger, rage, hostility as aggression), and found eight similar traits. Allport concluded that his subjective, idiographic method was valid.

Study of Values: an objective self-report test by Allport, Vernon and Lindzey (1960). Values are traits representing strong interests and motivations, and form the basis of the unifying philosophy of life, a criterion of maturity. Everyone has some of each value, but one or two dominate. The six are theoretical (truth, rational approach), economic (useful, practical), aesthetic (form, harmony, grace), social (relationships, altruism), political (power, influence, prestige in all areas) and religious (mystical, understanding the universe). It is a nomothetic test, showing Allport used group methods when appropriate.

practice.q: Is there a universality of facial expressions across cultures, or do they vary? Also explain how people express emotions in computer-mediated communication.
practice.answer:
Universality: studies of American and Chinese infants and adults found some basic emotions expressed by identical facial expressions in both cultures and age groups (Albright et al., 1997; Camras et al., 1998).

Variation: much evidence points to differences. Chinese infants showed less variety of expression than American and Japanese infants (Camras, 1998). A remote Namibian tribe's expressions did not match Americans', suggesting perceptions of emotion are not universal (Gendron et al., 2014). White 3-year-old girls smiled more than Chinese or Chinese-American girls, with maternal strictness and household size also mattering (Camras et al., 2006). US and Japanese adults recognised own-culture expressions better (Dailey et al., 2010), even on robot faces (Trovato et al., 2014). Easterners express emotion mainly with the eyes, Westerners with the eyebrows and mouth (Jack et al., 2012); Asian Facebook photos are less intense than American ones (Huang & Park, 2013). So basic expressions show some consistency, but their variety, intensity and recognition depend on culture and family.

Computer-mediated communication: a program reading faces at 30 frames per second recognised basic emotions accurately (Susskind et al., 2007). Dutch teenagers in chat rooms used more emoticons in social than task contexts, positive icons in positive situations and negative icons in negative ones (Derks et al., 2007). People therefore express emotions online much as they do face to face; one's own emoji use can be discussed in this light.

practice.q: Critically evaluate Allport's theory of personality.
practice.answer:
Weaknesses: apart from expressive behaviour, the theory has stimulated little research. Its idiographic approach ran counter to the nomothetic mainstream of psychology, and its focus on healthy adults clashed with clinical psychology's concern with neurotics and psychotics. Its concepts are hard to translate into testable propositions: how can functional autonomy or propriate striving be observed or manipulated in a laboratory? Allport never explained how an original motive becomes autonomous (e.g., how working for money becomes working for its own sake), so we cannot predict which motives will become autonomous. His exclusive emphasis on uniqueness makes it impossible to generalise from one person to another. Many reject his discontinuity between child and adult, animal and human, and normal and abnormal, since research on children, animals and disturbed people has taught much about healthy adults.

Strengths: many psychologists still see his views as a better basis for understanding personality than most theories (Piekkola, 2011). His ideas on development, uniqueness and goals influenced Maslow and Rogers, and he is seen as one of the first to bring humanistic values into psychology (Jeshmaridian, 2007). Current trait research supports some of his ideas; his work on emotional expression aided cognitive neuroscience; interest in personal documents has revived. His readable books, commonsense concepts, focus on conscious rational motives and future orientation offer a hopeful alternative to psychoanalysis. His most enduring contributions are making personality academically respectable and emphasising genetic factors in a trait approach.

practice.q: In what ways does Allport's theory of personality differ from Freud's? Discuss with reference to the unconscious, the past, research subjects, motivation and the goal of life.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Gordon Allport, who made personality an academically respectable field with his 1937 book, built his theory largely in opposition to Freud's psychoanalysis. His single traumatic meeting with Freud in Vienna, when Freud asked whether the dirt-fearing boy in Allport's story was Allport himself, convinced him that psychoanalysis probed the unconscious too deeply and that psychology should attend to conscious, visible motives. The differences can be organised under several headings.

1. Conscious versus unconscious

Freud held that unconscious forces dominate personality. Allport argued that emotionally healthy adults function rationally and consciously, aware of and in control of many of the forces motivating them. The unconscious, he said, is important only in neurotic or disturbed people. Correspondingly he stressed cognitive processes, conscious plans and intentions, as vital aspects of personality.

2. The past versus the present and future

Freud's historical determinism traced adult behaviour to childhood conflicts. Allport said we are not prisoners of the past; we are guided more by the present and our view of the future. Whatever happened in toilet training or school is past and inactive unless it still operates as a present force. His concept of functional autonomy states that adult motives become independent of the experiences in which they began, like a grown tree that no longer needs its seed. He also proposed two discontinuous personalities: a biologically driven infant and a psychologically functioning adult not constrained by childhood. Therefore adult motives cannot be understood by exploring childhood; we must ask why people behave as they do today.

3. Normal versus abnormal subjects

Freud built his theory on neurotic patients and saw a continuum between normal and abnormal. Allport saw a sharp break: the abnormal personality functions at an infantile level. He insisted on studying emotionally healthy adults and rejected comparisons with neurotics, children or animals. He also rejected methods suited to disturbed people: case studies focus on the past, and projective tests such as the TAT and Rorschach may distort normal personality by focusing on unconscious forces. He preferred asking people to describe themselves, personal documents and tests like the Study of Values.

4. Uniqueness versus universal laws

Freud proposed general laws of development applying to everyone. Allport emphasised the uniqueness of each personality, defined by personal dispositions, and favoured the idiographic study of individual cases.

5. Motivation and the goal of life

For Freud, the goal of life is tension reduction. Allport held the opposite: the ultimate goal is to increase tension, impelling us to seek new sensations and challenges. The reward lies in striving rather than arriving. He explained the present by the future: what we want and strive for is the key to behaviour.

6. Image of human nature

Freud's view was largely pessimistic and deterministic. Allport's was optimistic: adults consciously control their lives, plan for the future and are always in the process of becoming. He took a moderate stance on free will, granting free choice about the future while accepting that traits determine some behaviour.

Points of overlap

Allport did not reject childhood entirely: the infant-mother bond determines whether the proprium develops healthily, and frustrated needs produce a neurotic adult still governed by childhood drives, a view not far from Freud's for the disturbed personality.

Conclusion

Allport's theory reverses Freud on almost every major point: conscious over unconscious, future over past, healthy over disturbed, unique over universal, and tension increase over tension reduction. Critics argue that his discontinuity between child and adult, and normal and abnormal, ignores useful knowledge from studies of children and patients. Yet his rational, hopeful picture of human nature offered an important alternative to psychoanalysis and influenced humanistic psychologists such as Maslow and Rogers.

practice.q: Explain Allport's concept of functional autonomy. Describe its two levels and the three principles that govern propriate functional autonomy. What is the relationship between adult motives and childhood experiences?
practice.answer:
Introduction

Allport believed that the central problem for any personality theory is how it treats motivation. Emphasising the present and conscious intentions, he proposed functional autonomy, his best-known and most distinctive concept. It holds that the motives of mature, emotionally healthy adults are not functionally connected to the prior experiences in which they first appeared; they become autonomous, independent of their original circumstances.

Illustrations

Allport compared it to a tree, which can be traced to its seed but, once grown, no longer needs the seed for nourishment. Similarly, adults remain related to their parents but are no longer functionally dependent on them. In his career example, young graduates work hard to gain financial security. Decades later, with that goal achieved, some still work just as hard. Hard work, once a means to an end, has become an end in itself.

Two levels of functional autonomy

1. Perseverative functional autonomy is the more elementary level. It includes addictions and repetitive physical actions, such as habitual ways of doing routine tasks. These behaviours persist without external reward; they once served a purpose but no longer do, and are too low-level to be an integral part of personality. Evidence: a rat trained to run a maze for food may keep running it when well fed; humans prefer familiar routines that continue without reinforcement.

2. Propriate functional autonomy is the more important level and essential for understanding adult motivation. 'Propriate' comes from proprium, Allport's term for the self. It relates to values, self-image and lifestyle. Propriate motives are unique to each person. The ego decides which motives to keep, retaining those that enhance self-esteem and self-image, so we enjoy doing what we do well. A child forced into piano lessons out of fear of parental displeasure may, as skill grows, continue because playing has become necessary to his self-image.

The three principles of propriate functioning

Propriate functioning is an organising process that maintains our sense of self, selectively determining what we perceive, remember and think about in line with our interests and values. It follows three principles:

- Organizing the energy level: new motives are acquired out of necessity, to use surplus energy that might otherwise be expressed destructively, e.g., retired people should channel spare time into new interests.
- Mastery and competence: adequate achievement is not enough; mature adults are motivated to perform better, master new skills and increase competence.
- Propriate patterning: a striving for consistency and integration, organising perception and cognition around the self, keeping what enhances self-image and rejecting the rest.

Limits

Allport admitted that reflexes, fixations, neuroses and biologically driven behaviours are not controlled by functionally autonomous motives.

Adult motives and childhood experiences

In the healthy adult, motives are independent of childhood: the past is inactive unless it survives as a present force. Adult motives therefore cannot be understood by exploring childhood, as Freud believed, but by investigating present reasons and future goals. This reflects Allport's view of two discontinuous personalities. The exception is the neurotic: if childhood needs for affection and security were frustrated, motives do not become functionally autonomous but stay tied to their original conditions. The role of cognitive processes is central here: conscious intentions and plans, what we want and strive for, explain behaviour.

Evaluation and conclusion

Functional autonomy captures something real about adult life: activities begun for one reason often continue for quite different ones. Its link to Allport's own biography, his need to free himself from his brother Floyd's shadow, has been noted. However, critics argue that Allport never explained how an original motive is transformed into an autonomous one, so we cannot predict which motives will become autonomous, and the concept is very difficult to observe or manipulate in a laboratory. Nonetheless, it remains a key alternative to Freud's historical determinism and an optimistic statement that adults are free to shape their own motives.

practice.q: Describe the concept of the proprium and the seven stages of its development. What is the importance of the infant-mother bond, and how does the theory account for emotional disturbance in adulthood?
practice.answer:
Introduction

Allport used the term proprium for the self or ego, rejecting the words 'self' and 'ego' because other theorists had given them so many meanings. The term is best understood through the adjective 'appropriate': the proprium includes the aspects of personality that are distinctive and appropriate to our individual emotional life. These aspects are unique to each person and unite attitudes, perceptions and intentions. The proprium is also the basis of propriate functional autonomy, since the ego selects which motives are retained.

The infant before the proprium

The newborn has no self-consciousness and no separation of 'me' from everything else. Sensory impressions trigger automatic, reflexive responses with no ego mediating between stimulus and response. Allport described infants as pleasure seeking, destructive, selfish, impatient and dependent, 'unsocialized horrors' with little personality, driven by reflexes to reduce tension and maximise pleasure.

The seven stages (Table 7.1)

Stages 1-3 (first three years; birth to about 4):
1. Bodily self: awareness of a 'bodily me'; infants distinguish their own bodies, e.g., their fingers, from objects.
2. Self-identity: a sense of continuity; children realise they remain the same person despite changes in body and abilities, aided by learning their names and seeing themselves as distinct.
3. Self-esteem: pride in doing things on their own; a drive to build, explore and manipulate objects. If parents frustrate exploration, self-esteem may give way to humiliation and anger.

Stages 4-5 (ages 4-6):
4. Extension of self: awareness of objects and people as belonging to the child: 'my house', 'my parents', 'my school'.
5. Self-image: actual and ideal self-images form through interaction with parents, who convey their expectations and how far the child meets them.

Stage 6 (ages 6-12):
6. Self as a rational coper: realising that reason and logic can solve everyday problems.

Stage 7 (adolescence):
7. Propriate striving: forming long-range plans and goals; until this happens the proprium remains incomplete.

Adulthood: normal mature adults are functionally autonomous, independent of childhood motives, function rationally in the present and consciously create their own lifestyles.

The infant-mother bond

Interaction with parents matters throughout, but the infant-mother bond, as a source of affection and security, is most important of all. If the mother or primary caregiver provides sufficient affection and security, the proprium develops gradually and steadily and the child grows psychologically. Childhood motives can then be transformed into the autonomous propriate strivings of adulthood, a pattern of personal dispositions forms, and the result is a mature, emotionally healthy adult.

Emotional disturbance in adulthood

If childhood needs are frustrated, the self does not mature properly. The child becomes insecure, aggressive, demanding, jealous and self-centred, and growth is stunted. The result is a neurotic adult who functions at the level of childhood drives. Such an adult's motives do not become functionally autonomous but remain tied to their original conditions; traits and personal dispositions fail to develop, and the personality remains undifferentiated, as in infancy. This fits Allport's statements that the abnormal personality functions at an infantile level and that the unconscious and past matter mainly in neurotic people.

Conclusion

The proprium is the developing core of the unique self, built in seven stages from bodily awareness to future-oriented striving. Allport's account gives parents, especially the mother, a crucial role. An interesting tension is that although he denied the influence of childhood on healthy adults, whether one becomes healthy at all depends on early affection and security. The stages also connect to his criteria of maturity, for example extension of self and the future goals expressed in a unifying philosophy of life.

practice.q: What are the characteristics of the mature, healthy adult personality according to Allport? Relate them to his view of human nature and the ultimate goal of life.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Allport studied normal, emotionally healthy adults rather than neurotic patients, so his description of the mature personality is central to his theory. He saw healthy development as a change from a biologically dominated organism in infancy to a mature psychological organism in adulthood, whose motives are separated from childhood and oriented toward the future. If childhood needs for affection and security were met, the proprium develops satisfactorily and the adult is no longer dominated by childhood drives.

The six criteria of maturity

1. Extension of the sense of self: mature adults extend their sense of self to people and activities beyond themselves, genuinely participating in work, family, friendships and causes. This continues the childhood stage of extension of self.

2. Warm relating to others: they relate warmly, showing intimacy, compassion and tolerance.

3. Self-acceptance and emotional security: a high degree of self-acceptance helps them achieve emotional security.

4. Realistic perception, skills and commitment to work: they perceive life realistically, develop personal skills and commit themselves to some type of work. This echoes the principle of mastery and competence.

5. Humour and self-objectification: they have a sense of humour and self-objectification, an understanding of or insight into themselves.

6. A unifying philosophy of life: this directs the personality toward future goals. Allport, Vernon and Lindzey proposed that personal values (theoretical, economic, aesthetic, social, political, religious), measured by the Study of Values, are the basis of this philosophy.

Adults meeting these criteria are emotionally healthy and functionally autonomous, independent of childhood motives; they cope with the present and plan for the future without being victims of their early years.

Link to human nature

These criteria express Allport's optimistic image of human nature: adults in conscious control of their lives, attending rationally to current situations, planning ahead and actively fashioning an identity. We are always in the process of becoming, creatively designing a lifestyle shaped more by present and future than by the past. On free will, he was moderate: we choose freely about the future, though traits and personal dispositions, once formed, determine some behaviour and are hard to change. On nature and nurture, genes supply physique, temperament and intelligence, shaped by learning and experience. On uniqueness, personal dispositions describe us more precisely than common traits.

The ultimate goal of life

Unlike Freud's tension reduction, Allport held that the ultimate and necessary goal of life is to increase tension, impelling us to keep seeking new sensations and challenges. Having met one challenge, we seek another. The reward is the process of achieving rather than the achievement: 'getting there is more fun than being there'. We need new goals constantly to maintain an optimal level of tension. This fits the mature personality: commitment to work, mastery of skills and a philosophy directing us toward future goals are exactly how this continual striving is achieved.

Allport the person

His optimism was reflected in his liberal stance, interest in social reform and a humanistic attitude mirrored in his personality; colleagues described him as genuinely caring about people.

Conclusion

Allport's mature personality is outward-looking, warm, secure, realistic, self-aware and guided by a unifying philosophy. Together with his view of life as continuous striving, it offers a hopeful picture that anticipated humanistic psychologists such as Maslow and Rogers. Critics may note that it is descriptive and hard to test empirically, but it remains a useful framework for understanding psychological health.

practice.q: Describe the research findings on how expressive behavior reveals aspects of personality.
practice.answer:
Introduction

Although Allport's theory as a whole generated little research, his concept of expressive behavior has stimulated a large and productive body of work. Allport distinguished expressive behavior, which is spontaneous, seemingly purposeless, hard to change and usually outside awareness, from coping behavior, which is consciously planned, purposeful and aimed at changing the environment. In public speaking, the lecture content is coping behavior, while the speaker's gestures, pacing, rapid speech or fidgeting are expressive and reveal personality.

Allport's own research

In his landmark study, Allport and Vernon (1933) gave subjects various tasks and found high consistency across situations in voice, handwriting, posture and gestures, from which traits such as introversion and extraversion could be inferred.

Assessing personality from expressive cues

Later work shows personality can be assessed from voice recordings, films, videotapes and even still photographs; facial expressions, vocal inflections and idiosyncratic gestures reveal traits to trained observers (Russell et al., 2003; Berry, 1990; DePaulo, 1993). Some people form reliable impressions of strangers from facial appearance alone (Berry & Wero, 1993), and observers accurately judged anxiety from under 30 seconds of film (Ambody & Rosenthal, 1992).

Gender, age and experience

Women and younger people recognise facial emotions better than men and older people (Sasson et al., 2010); children read expressions from age 5 (Gao & Maurer, 2010). Women with positive expressions in yearbook photos at 21 reported greater well-being at 27, 43 and 52 and better marriages (Harker & Keltner, 2001). Abused children identified anger more readily (Pollak & Sinha, 2002). Depressed adults needed more intense faces to see happiness but less to see sadness (Joormann & Gotlib, 2006) and were better at recognising sadness; socially anxious children interpreted expressions better (Ale et al., 2010; Gollan et al., 2010). Japanese children who played more video games recognised expressions better (Tamamiya & Jiraki, 2013), and close friends decode emotions far better than acquaintances (Zhang & Parmley, 2011).

Coding facial expressions

Paul Ekman identified seven distinguishable facial emotions: anger, contempt, disgust, fear, sadness, surprise and happiness (Ekman et al., 1997). His Facial Action Coding System, based on 43 muscles and 3,000 configurations, is used by police, the CIA and FBI to detect lying (Kaufman, 2002). Keltner (1997) linked neuroticism to anger, contempt and fear; agreeableness to laughter; extraversion to smiles and amusement; and conscientiousness to embarrassment. We recognise smiles by unconsciously mimicking them (Niedenthal et al., 2010).

Emotional states

Type A people show disgust, glaring, grimacing and scowling (Chesney et al., 1997); facial expressions distinguished depressed Swiss patients who later attempted suicide (Heller & Haynal, 1997); highly anxious Japanese students showed distinct expressions around the mouth and left side of the face (Nakamura, 2002).

Culture and computers

Some basic emotions look alike in American and Chinese faces (Albright et al., 1997), but many studies show cultural differences in variety, intensity, facial regions used (eyes in the East, eyebrows and mouth in the West; Jack et al., 2012) and own-culture recognition advantages (Dailey et al., 2010). Computers can recognise basic emotions from video at 30 frames per second (Susskind et al., 2007), and teenagers use emoticons online much as they use facial expressions face to face (Derks et al., 2007).

Conclusion

Taken together, these findings provide strong support for Allport's proposition that expressive behavior reflects personality traits. They show that traits and emotional states can be read from faces, voices and gestures, that this skill varies with gender, age, experience, emotional state and culture, and that it can even be automated. Allport's work on emotional expression has been described as vitally important for the development of cognitive neuroscience.
